title: He Came Off the Bench With 14 Minutes Left. Cyle Larin Gave Canada Its First World Cup Point — Ever.
excerpt: In front of 43,000 fans at Toronto’s BMO Field, Larin’s 78th-minute equalizer against Bosnia rescued a historic 1-1 draw and ended Canada’s seven-game World Cup losing streak.
body:
When the final whistle blew at BMO Field on Friday evening, the roar that erupted from 43,000 throats in Toronto carried the weight of four decades. Canada had earned its first-ever World Cup point. One single point — scraped, clawed, and ultimately conjured from the right boot of a substitute who had been on the pitch for barely two minutes.

Cyle Larin, the Brampton-born striker who Southampton fans had watched toil without reward for much of the English season, came off the bench in the 76th minute of Canada’s Group B opener against Bosnia and Herzegovina. One hundred and twenty-one seconds later, he swivelled in the box and fired a shot past Nikola Vasilj to send the stands into delirium. The scoreboard read 1-1. It might as well have read *history*.

## The Long Wait

Before Friday, Canada’s World Cup record read: played six, lost six. The 1986 squad in Mexico was shut out in all three group games. The 2022 vintage in Qatar fared little better, managing a single Alphonso Davies goal against Croatia before exiting winless. A losing streak stretching across seven consecutive World Cup matches, spanning 36 years, had calcified into something close to accepted fate.

That burden sat heavy on Jesse Marsch’s team from the opening whistle. The occasion was enormous — Canada’s first-ever World Cup match on home soil, preceded by an opening ceremony that featured Michael Bublé, Alanis Morissette, and Bollywood-crossover star Nora Fatehi performing the official tournament anthem *Siir Siir* to a sea of red-clad fans. The atmosphere was electric. The football, initially, was not.

## Bosnia Strike First

Bosnia and Herzegovina, making only their second World Cup appearance after Brazil 2014, showed no reverence for the occasion. In the 21st minute, Ivan Basic delivered a corner that Sead Kolasinac flicked on, and Jovo Lukic met it with a thumping header that beat Maxime Crepeau and silenced the stadium. It was Lukic’s first-ever international goal, scored against the tournament’s co-hosts in front of their own fans.

The setback could have broken Canada. Instead, it galvanized them.

## Dominance Without Reward

From that point forward, Marsch’s men dominated possession — finishing with 64% of the ball — and peppered the Bosnian goal with crosses, through-balls, and half-chances that refused to convert. Jonathan David, Canada’s all-time leading scorer, had an early sight of goal from the center of the area but fired straight at Vasilj. Tani Oluwaseyi blazed over from promising positions.

The cruelest moment came in the 53rd minute, when Richie Laryea surged through on goal and beat the goalkeeper, only for Kolasinac to produce one of the tournament’s early iconic moments — a desperate goal-line clearance that ricocheted off the crossbar and back into play. The stadium groaned. The scoreboard stubbornly refused to change.

As the minutes drained away, BMO Field — temporarily renamed Toronto Stadium for the tournament, its capacity boosted from 28,000 to over 43,000 with temporary seating at each end — grew quieter. Even Ryan Reynolds, the Wrexham owner and Canadian expat watching from the stands, wore a grimace.

## Larin’s Moment

Then Marsch made his move. Larin and Promise David replaced the tiring forwards, and within moments, the gamble paid off. Ismaël Koné drove toward the center of the penalty area and laid a pass to David, who found Larin standing with his back to goal. One touch to control. A swivel. A prod with the outside of his right foot into the bottom corner. Seventy-eight minutes played, first touch of the game — and Canada had their equalizer.

The first-ever World Cup goal on Canadian soil, as the camera panned across fans in tears, with Bosnian protests that Larin had handled the ball dismissed by VAR in Dallas.

## What It Means for NRIs in Canada

For the estimated 1.8 million South Asians living in the Greater Toronto Area — the largest desi diaspora concentration in North America — Friday was more than a football match. It was a shared civic moment in their adopted home, amplified by the presence of Nora Fatehi, the Canadian-born Bollywood actress of Moroccan descent, on the opening ceremony stage.

The World Cup descends next on Vancouver, where Canada face Qatar on Thursday, June 18 at BC Place — another city with a massive Punjabi and South Asian community. A win there would almost certainly send Canada through to the Round of 32 for the first time in the nation’s history. For NRIs who have watched this country grow from a footballing afterthought into a co-host of the world’s biggest sporting event, the stakes feel deeply personal.

Viewers in India can catch the remaining Group B fixtures on Sports18 and JioTV, with the Qatar match kicking off at 3:30 AM IST — an hour made slightly more bearable by the possibility of witnessing something unprecedented.

## Looking Ahead

Canada sit second in Group B behind Switzerland (who face Qatar on Saturday at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara). Bosnia, who will rue Kolasinac’s heroics not being enough, play Switzerland next on Thursday.

For Larin, the man whose 14-goal international drought had made him a target of fan frustration — one supporter tweeted “couldn’t be more happier” when his name was left off the starting XI — Friday offered the sweetest possible redemption. He needed 121 seconds and a single touch to rewrite a 40-year narrative.

Canada have a World Cup point. Now they want more.
